Main topics: continuous batching behavior, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, max_batch_tokens, batch_fill_ms), token limits and truncation strategies, KV cache priming/warmup, quantization tradeoffs for throughput vs quality, and VPC/on-prem networking constraints. transcript:
00:00 Samir Patel: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to set aside an hour to go deep on throughput tuning for the BrightScale use case. we'll do intros quick and then jump into your current infra and goals.
00:12 Jordan Lee: Hi Samir, Jordan here, CTO at BrightScale. we've got Priya, Marcus and Ellen on as well.
00:18 Priya Raman: hey all, Priya, Head of ML.
00:21 Marcus Wu: Marcus, infra.
:24 Ellen Park: Ellen, SRE.
00:26 Samir Patel: Great thanks. Lina from Redwood is joining to walk scheduler knobs and Tom will cover quantization effects. Lina you wanna start with the continuous batching explanation?
00:36 Lina Gomez: sure — quick TL;DR: continuous batching lets the runtime accumulate live requests into batches up to policy thresholds (max_num_seqs, max_batch_tokens) or time windows (batch_fill_ms). the scheduler then decides when to dispatch to GPU. for throughput-heavy apps the trick is balancing fill latency vs batch efficiency.
00:56 Jordan Lee: our primary KPI is 2000 requests/min with 95th latency under 400ms for inference-only endpoints. currently using 8k context, average prompt length 150 tokens, response average 60 tokens.
01:10 Priya Raman: also many short bursts — product usage has microbursts of 200-300 qps for 30s then idle.
01:18 Tom Hsu: ok that burstiness pattern matters — continuous batching with a conservative batch_fill_ms helps smooth bursts without creating large latency spikes. one common starting point is batch_fill_ms=10–25ms and max_num_seqs tuned to expected concurrency.
01:33 Marcus Wu: quick Q — what about max_num_seqs exactly? our current Redwood default is 64 sequences per batch but we've seen queuing at peak.
01:42 Lina Gomez: max_num_seqs limits number of sequences (requests) in a single batch. if your requests are short, you can set it higher; if they're long or you want stable p95, keep it lower. for your 150 token prompts + 60 token responses, effective token-per-seq ~210, so max_num_seqs=64 gives ~13.4k tokens which for some kernels is large and may affect kernel selection and memory.
02:05 Ellen Park: kernel selection? can it OOM?
02:08 Lina Gomez: yes, the runtime picks kernels based on sequence length and batch tokens. there's an internal threshold; very wide batches can force different memory paths and reduce perf or risk OOM on smaller GPUs. we usually tune max_batch_tokens rather than only num_seqs. set max_batch_tokens to something like 10k–14k depending on GPU memory.
02:27 Jordan Lee: what about token limits and truncation — we sometimes get very long prompts when customers paste documents.
02:33 Tom Hsu: recommended pattern: enforce an ingress token cap at the gateway, truncate or summarize long user inputs, and use per-request max_output_tokens. you can also surface a rejection path for very long sequences.
02:44 Priya Raman: do you support streaming in that scenario? streaming complicates batching right?
02:49 Lina Gomez: streaming is supported; continuous batching still batches across streams but we prioritize latency — streaming responses often flush earlier. there's a tradeoff: streaming reduces batch efficiency but improves per-request latency. for BrightScale we might use streaming for web interactive flows and non-stream for backend bulk scoring.
03:06 Marcus Wu: KV cache — our clients reuse conversations, can cache help throughput?
03:10 Lina Gomez: yes, KV cache is a big win. for repeated prefixes KV caching avoids recomputing earlier keys. but cache hit-rate is critical — warmup strategies matter. if your traffic is diverse you get fewer hits. for conversation apps with repeated user history, expect 2–3x token throughput improvement on cached steps.
03:29 Ellen Park: how do you warm caches on Dedicated or private deployments? we want deterministic cold-start behavior.
03:34 Lina Gomez: we offer cache priming APIs and ability to pre-warm by replaying representative prefixes during low-traffic windows. on Dedicated clusters you can allocate persistent KV stores per-deployment for higher hit rates. also TTL controls let you keep hot prefixes longer.
03:49 Jordan Lee: scheduler knobs again — batch_fill_ms, max_batch_tokens, max_num_seqs — any recommended defaults for our goal (2000rpm, p95 < 400ms)?
03:58 Tom Hsu: start with batch_fill_ms=15ms, max_num_seqs=32, max_batch_tokens=12000. then run benchmarks. If p95 too high, drop max_num_seqs to 16 and reduce batch_fill_ms to 8ms to favor latency; if throughput under target, increase max_num_seqs to 48 and batch_fill_ms up to 30ms to improve batch packing.
04:21 Priya Raman: we plan to run a pilot on our VMs in our VPC with a private deployment. any networking caveats?
04:27 Lina Gomez: VPC/on-prem adds egress and latency constraints. ensure local L4 load balancer has affinity settings consistent so requests from same session hit same node for cache locality, or use a redis-backed shared KV if you need cross-node cache. also watch MTU and encryption overhead — for high qps TLS can add CPU overhead if not offloaded.
04:47 Marcus Wu: affinity — we use AWS NLB now. is session stickiness necessary?
04:51 Tom Hsu: recommended for KV cache benefits. without stickiness shared KV store works but introduces extra network hop; depending on your infra you may get better p95 by packing user sessions to nodes.
05:02 Jordan Lee: quantization — how much throughput improvement vs quality loss? we need numbers for our model family (Redwood suggested smaller LLM ~7B?).
05:10 Tom Hsu: for transformer-family 7B variants: int8 quantization can often yield 1.8–2.5x token throughput improvement and 20–40% GPU memory reduction. quality regressions are model-dependent — usually small on opt-like models but you should run evals. per-token latency also drops. we also support mixed-precision pathways; sometimes int8 + kernel tuning hits best cost curve.
05:36 Priya Raman: can we do A/B between float16 and int8 during pilot?
05:39 Lina Gomez: yes — the runtime supports variant rollouts and automatic fallback. we can register two model variants and route a percentage to quantized model for live A/B. logs will capture token-level differences so you can evaluate.
05:51 Ellen Park: security/compliance — if we do private, how do you handle KMS and key material?
05:55 Samir Patel: Redwood Private integrates with customer KMS/HSM, we don't hold keys in hosted Private control plane. we can provide SOC2 docs; we'll send security pack after call.
06:05 Jordan Lee: great. any quick wins to prototype before the benchmark run?
06:09 Lina Gomez: yes — set an ingress token cap, reduce default max_num_seqs to 32, and enable KV caching for conversation endpoints. also set batch_fill_ms to 15ms. these are low-risk and reversible.
06:20 Priya Raman: we worry about token limits for analytics flows — batch scoring thousands of short docs. are batched doc scoring patterns different?
06:28 Tom Hsu: short-doc scoring benefits from raising max_num_seqs since token-per-seq is small. set max_num_seqs high (128 or 256) but cap max_batch_tokens to protect memory. also enable dynamic padding minimization (we provide an option to group sequences by length bucket).
06:47 Marcus Wu: dynamic padding — any caveats for GPU kernel selection?
06:51 Lina Gomez: grouping by length reduces wasted compute but can increase scheduling complexity; there is a slight scheduler overhead but net throughput usually wins. kernels selected will be for the bucket length.
07:02 Jordan Lee: let's recap action items and schedule the benchmark.
07:05 Samir Patel: recap: Samir will run perf benchmark using your sample prompts (Priya to share), Lina will send recommended knob values and a short tuning guide, Tom will include quantization A/B plan, and Priya will share traffic profile. We'll aim to have benchmark results by Friday.
07:21 Priya Raman: sounds good. we'll share the data by tomorrow.
07:25 Ellen Park: thanks team.
07:27 Samir Patel: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invite and docs.
07:31 [call ends]
